client: Hi Luna, I've been really struggling lately with my recent promotion. The added responsibilities are making me doubt my abilities, and I feel like I'm constantly overwhelmed. I'm not even sure if therapy can really help with something like this.
therapist: Hi there, it sounds like you're going through a really tough time with your promotion. It's completely normal to feel overwhelmed and doubt your abilities when faced with new challenges. Therapy can definitely help you work through these feelings and build your confidence. How have you been coping with these feelings so far?

client: I've mostly been trying to keep up by working longer hours and relying on caffeine to get through the day. But it feels like no matter how much I do, I can't shake this constant worry that I'm not good enough for the job. It's really taking a toll on me.
therapist: It sounds like you're putting a lot of pressure on yourself to keep up, and the long hours and caffeine are taking a toll. It's understandable to feel like you're not good enough, but it's important to recognize that these feelings are often part of the adjustment to new roles. What are some thoughts or evidence that come to mind when you doubt your abilities?

client: When I doubt my abilities, I keep thinking about all the times I've made mistakes or felt unsure. I compare myself to my colleagues who seem so confident and competent. It's hard to shake the feeling that I'm the only one who isn't handling this well.
therapist: It's really tough to feel like you're not measuring up, especially when you see others seeming so confident. It's important to remember that everyone has their own struggles, even if they're not visible on the surface. Can you think of any times when you've handled challenges well or received positive feedback that might help balance these negative thoughts?

client: I do remember a few times when my manager praised me for my work, especially on some recent projects. But those moments feel few and far between, and the negative thoughts tend to overshadow them. It's hard to hold onto those positive moments when the self-doubt is so strong.
therapist: It's completely understandable that the negative thoughts can overshadow the positive ones, especially when you're feeling overwhelmed. It's great that you can recall those moments of praise and success, even if they feel few and far between. How do you think we could make those positive moments more visible to you, so they can start to balance out the self-doubt?

client: I don't think that will work for me, Luna. It's hard because the self-doubt is so persistent, and those positive moments feel so distant. I worry that even if I try to focus on them, the negative thoughts will just keep coming back. How do I stop the cycle of doubt?
therapist: I understand that the self-doubt can feel very persistent and overwhelming. It's natural to worry that focusing on positive moments might not be enough to stop the cycle. One strategy that can help is to create a more structured way to balance out those negative thoughts. For example, you could keep a daily journal of three things you did well or received positive feedback on, no matter how small. This can help reinforce the positive and make it easier to recall them when self-doubt creeps in. What do you think about trying that approach?

client: I appreciate the suggestion, Luna, but it feels like another task on an already overwhelming to-do list. I worry that keeping a journal will just add more pressure and won't actually help me feel better. It's hard to see how writing things down will change the way I feel when the doubts are so ingrained.
therapist: I completely understand that adding another task to your already overwhelming list can feel daunting. It's important to find a balance that doesn't add to your stress. Instead of journaling, we could try a different approach, like setting aside a few minutes each day to reflect on one positive thing that happened, without writing it down. This can help shift your focus without feeling like an additional burden. How does that sound to you?

client: That sounds a bit more manageable, Luna. I think I could try to take a few minutes to reflect on something positive each day. I'm still a bit skeptical about how much it will help, but I'm willing to give it a shot. Thanks for understanding and suggesting a lighter approach.
therapist: I'm glad that the lighter approach feels more manageable for you. It's okay to be a bit skeptical; trying something new can be challenging. Taking a few minutes to reflect on something positive each day can be a gentle way to start shifting your perspective. How do you think you might fit this reflection time into your daily routine?

client: I think I could try to fit this reflection time into my evening routine, maybe right before bed. It feels like a good way to end the day on a positive note, but I'm still a bit worried about whether I'll actually stick with it. I tend to struggle with consistency, especially when I'm feeling overwhelmed.
therapist: That's a great idea to incorporate the reflection time into your evening routine. Ending the day on a positive note can be really helpful. It's totally normal to worry about consistency, especially when you're feeling overwhelmed. One way to make it easier might be to set a small, achievable goal, like reflecting on one positive thing for just a minute or two. How does that feel to you?

client: That feels more doable, Luna. Reflecting for just a minute or two seems like something I could manage. I'll give it a try and see how it goes. It's still a bit daunting, but I appreciate your support and the smaller goal.
therapist: I'm glad that reflecting for just a minute or two feels more doable for you. It's great that you're willing to give it a try, even if it still feels a bit daunting. Taking small steps can make a big difference over time. How do you think you'll remind yourself to take that minute each evening?

client: I think I could set a reminder on my phone to go off around the same time each evening. It's a good way to make sure I don't forget, and it feels like a gentle nudge rather than another task. I'll give it a try and see how it goes.
therapist: Setting a reminder on your phone is a great idea! It can serve as a gentle nudge to help you stay consistent without feeling like an additional task. It's wonderful that you're taking this step, and I'm here to support you as you try it out. How do you feel about giving it a week and then reflecting on how it's going?
